messages.body_plain:
Cheryl
I think you may be applying 'openCR' thinking in 'secr', which doesn't always work. In openCR 't' is a synonym of (primary) 'session'. In secr, 't' refers to occasions within a (primary) session (secondary sessions in Pollock terminology), and you cannot model density as varying within a (primary) session (it's closed i.e. constant).

All I'm saying is that it may work if you use D~session instead of D~t.

I'd love to know if you've really found a bug in 4.4.7. I have been working on a significant bug for Poisson count data that Ian Durbach turned up today, and expect to put out a patched version in a couple of days.
Murray

Hello and thank you Murray,

I managed to run hybrid mixture models with the sex partially known.
But now I doubt about the choice of the best detection model. Here the AIC comparisons, first with constant density :

And then with density varying across sessions :
> AIC(Dsess, Dsess.sig0, Dsess.sig, Dsess.g0)
                                 model            detectfn npar    logLik       AIC       AICc      dAICc   AICcwt

Values of the parameters are consistent with the density constant or not, sigma and g0 higher for male, and the sex ratio is plausible.

Questions:
1/ Is it relevant to look for the best detection model first and to use it for the density modelling ? Should I try in the other way to see if there is any differences ?
2/ Should I model-average the first two model ? How to do it to then look for the best density parametrization ? Maybe fixing values of g0 and sigma, but I d'ont know how to do it for different sessions. Or should I choose the model with sigma and g0 modelled with the sex covariate because it seems logical to me despite the AIC ? How to justify it ?
3/ Any remark or advise ?

Thank you
Yon

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We are conducting a spatial mark resight analysis via camera traps for a large carnivore. Our goal is to compare camera trapping abundance estimates to the current method that is used to obtain abundance. As such, we are interested in obtaining a reliable estimate of N from our SMR models. We compared AIC between 4 models and our null model was the most supported, with the following region.N() estimate.

fit0 <- secr.fit(CH, mask = HabitatMaskBuffer, trace = FALSE, details = list(knownmarks = FALSE))

null.model <- secr.fit(CH, detectfn = 'HN', model = list(D = ~1, g0= ~1, sigma = ~1), mask =  HabitatMaskBuffer  , trace = FALSE, start = fit0, details = list(knownmarks = FALSE, nsim = 10000))

region.N(null.model)
           estimate     SE.estimate        lcl                    ucl              n
E.N     94.07610     10.654746     75.40186     117.37525     37
R.N     68.88342     4.409934       61.34383     78.75812       37

We are concerned because of the large difference between EN and RN. We reviewed previous posts on this group such as this <https://groups.google.com/g/secrgroup/c/cTn-tb8If-g/m/efU_2hKSEQAJ> and this <https://groups.google.com/g/secrgroup/c/FcB8f4rB1Qg/m/PdOiyr-LUbwJ> but have additional questions. Specifically, because the above results are from our null model, where density is flat (D ~ 1) and g0 ~ 1, we are stumped why our EN and RN estimates differ. Is this a possible limitation of SMR? We are seeking advice on the potential cause and solutions to move forward.

Thank you for your insight.

messages.subject_clean: EN and RN discrepancy
messages.body_plain:
Yes, there is a persistent discrepancy in region.N for all-sighting data with knownmarks = FALSE. RN is defined as the sum of the actual number detected (n) and the expected number that the model says would not be detected, given the estimated total density. Unfortunately (by my oversight) the second component (expected number not detected) is calculated in region.N by applying the wrong 'probability of being missed'. It uses the probability of being missed _conditional on being individually identifiable_ (marked). The calculation should use the unconditional probability of being missed (i.e. allowing for the proportion of animals that were unmarked and intrinsically unidentifiable). We don't estimate the proportion marked as such, and the best estimate is exactly RN = EN. I'm not so sure about the SE, but it's probably closer to 10.65 than 4.4.

messages.body_plain:
I've only taken a quick look, but your openCR model has a problem (SE 0 for superD). Also, superD is cumulative across time, so generally should not be compared to time-specific density.

reduce(data, by='all') collapses data to a capthist object of the same detector type on a single occasion, which in the case of binary proximity detectors results in (large) loss of information. Perhaps this is why openCR fails. You may want to specify outputdetector = 'count'; then with binomN = 1 openCR.fit() fits a binomial model to the resulting counts (size of binomial from usage attribute). (You could try that also in secr).

I indicated earlier my distaste for using openCR to estimate density. There may be times when it's needed, but there are many more things that can go wrong. You are modelling or making assumptions about not just phi but also recruitment and movement between sessions (activity centres probably not static), and any of these may vary over time. Subtle breaches of assumptions (e.g. unmodelled heterogeneity) can generate patterns over time (historically , for nonspatial JS, downturns either end).
